answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is Mary Shelley’s own wording, confirmed in Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus (1818) — though in the novel it is spoken by the Creature to Victor Frankenstein, not by Shelley in her own voice.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Vol. III, Ch. III (1818 text) / Chapter 20 (1831 revised numbering)

source.excerpt: You can blast my other passions; but revenge remains—revenge, henceforth dearer than light or food! I may die; but first you, my tyrant and tormentor, shall curse the sun that gazes on your misery. Beware; for I am fearless, and therefore powerful. I will watch with the wiliness of a snake, that I may sting with its venom. Man, you shall repent of the injuries you inflict.
trail: First published anonymously as Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus ↗ (London: Lackington, Hughes, Harding, Mavor & Jones, 1818), written when Mary Shelley was eighteen to twenty years old.
The exact line is confirmed in Volume III, Chapter III of the 1818 first-edition text via a full chapter transcription ↗.
The same wording is unchanged in Chapter 20 of the 1831 revised edition ↗.

Despite its life as inspirational merchandise, the line does not appear among the curated highlights on Mary Shelley’s Wikiquote page ↗ — a reminder of how far it has drifted from its original, darker context.
source.excerptNote: Spoken after Victor destroys the unfinished female companion he had promised to create — this is a threat of revenge, not a personal statement by Shelley.
source.rightsNote: Frankenstein was first published in 1818, well before the 1931 threshold, and Mary Shelley died in 1851 — both the original text and her later 1831 revision are in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Mary Shelley
author.heading: About Mary Shelley
author.bio: Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley wrote Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus at eighteen and nineteen, publishing it anonymously in 1818 when she was twenty. Daughter of philosophers William Godwin and Mary Wollstonecraft, and wife of poet Percy Bysshe Shelley, she went on to write further novels, short stories, and travel writing, and edited her husband’s posthumous work.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The authorship here isn’t in doubt — Mary Shelley wrote every word of this line. What’s misleading is the context it’s stripped of when it circulates as a standalone inspirational quote.

items.who: Popular "empowerment" quote cards, prints, and notebooks
items.why: Widely sold and shared as if it were Mary Shelley speaking in her own voice about her own fearlessness, when it is in fact dialogue from a fictional character — the Creature — delivering a threat of revenge against his creator.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are genuinely Mary Shelley’s, confirmed in the primary text of Frankenstein, Vol. III, Ch. III ↗ — but they belong to the Creature, mid-threat, not to Shelley speaking for herself.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line comes near the novel’s climax, just after Victor Frankenstein destroys the half-finished female companion he had promised to build for his Creature. Devastated and enraged, the Creature confronts him on a desolate stretch of the Orkney coast, ending a long speech of grief and threat with: “You can blast my other passions; but revenge remains—revenge, henceforth dearer than light or food! I may die; but first you, my tyrant and tormentor, shall curse the sun that gazes on your misery. Beware; for I am fearless, and therefore powerful.”

In its original context, then, this is not a personal motto of Mary Shelley’s but a villain’s vow of vengeance — which makes its popular modern life as an inspirational, empowerment-themed quote (printed on notebooks, prints, and posters) something of an irony. The words are genuinely Shelley’s own prose, just not her own voice.
detailsBody: Frankenstein was published anonymously in three volumes on 1 January 1818; Mary Shelley was not credited by name on an English title page until the second edition of 1823.
Shelley substantially revised the novel for a single-volume 1831 edition. The “Beware; for I am fearless, and therefore powerful” line is unchanged between the 1818 and 1831 texts.
context.pull: In the novel it is the Creature’s threat of revenge — not Mary Shelley’s personal creed.
